etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English meten, from Old English mētan (“to meet, find, encounter”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōtijan (“to meet”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to come, meet”).

definitions.definition: To come face to face with by accident; to encounter.

quote.citation: 1899, Hughes Mearns, Antigonish:
quote.text: Yesterday, upon the stairI met a man who wasn’t thereHe wasn’t there again todayI wish, I wish he’d go away […]

definitions.definition: To come face to face with someone by arrangement.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 10, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: With a little manœuvring they contrived to meet on the doorstep which was  […]  in a boiling stream of passers-by, hurrying business people speeding past in a flurry of fumes and dust in the bright haze.

definitions.definition: To get acquainted with someone.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Captain Edward Carlisle […] felt a curious sensation of helplessness seize upon him as he met her steady gaze, […]; he could not tell what this prisoner might do. He cursed the fate which had assigned such a duty, cursed especially that fate which forced a gallant soldier to meet so superb a woman as this under handicap so hard.

definitions.definition: To make contact (with someone) while in proximity.
To gather for a formal or social discussion; to hold a meeting.

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, chapter III, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: At half-past nine on this Saturday evening, the parlour of the Salutation Inn, High Holborn, contained most of its customary visitors. […] In former days every tavern of repute kept such a room for its own select circle, a club, or society, of habitués, who met every evening, for a pipe and a cheerful glass.

definitions.definition: To come together in conflict.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, chapter LV, in Le Morte Darthur, book X:
quote.text: Sir said Epynegrys is þt the rule of yow arraunt knyghtes for to make a knyght to Iuste will he or nyllAs for that sayd Dynadan make the redyfor here is for meAnd there with al they spored theyr horses & mett to gyders soo hard that Epynegrys smote doune sir Dynadan(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VI”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Weapons more violent, when next we meet,May serve to better us and worse our foes.

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, Gary Younge, “Hypocrisy lies at heart of Manning prosecution”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 18:
quote.text: The dispatches […]  also exposed the blatant discrepancy between the west's professed values and actual foreign policies. Having lectured the Arab world about democracy for years, its collusion in suppressing freedom was undeniable as protesters were met by weaponry and tear gas made in the west, employed by a military trained by westerners.

definitions.definition: (sports) To play a match.
(Of groups) To come together.
To converge and finally touch or intersect.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Captain Edward Carlisle, soldier as he was, martinet as he was, felt a curious sensation of helplessness seize upon him as he met her steady gaze, her alluring smile; he could not tell what this prisoner might do

definitions.definition: To touch or hit something while moving.
To adjoin, be physically touching.
(transitive) To respond to (an argument etc.) with something equally convincing; to refute.
To make physical or perceptual contact.
To satisfy; to comply with.

quote.citation: 2013 June 22, “Engineers of a different kind”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8841, page 70:
quote.text: Private-equity nabobs bristle at being dubbed mere financiers. […] Much of their pleading is public-relations bluster. Clever financial ploys are what have made billionaires of the industry’s veterans. “Operational improvement” in a portfolio company has often meant little more than promising colossal bonuses to sitting chief executives if they meet ambitious growth targets. That model is still prevalent today.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To balance or come out correct.

quote.citation: 1967, Northern Ireland. Parliament. House of Commons, Parliamentary Debates (Hansard) House of Commons Official Report
quote.text: In this instance he has chosen an accountant. I suppose that it will be possible for an accountant to make the figures meet.

definitions.definition: To perceive; to come to a knowledge of; to have personal acquaintance with; to experience; to suffer.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], (please specify |epistle=I to IV), London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Of vice or virtue, whether blest or curst,Which meets contempt, or which compassion first.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXIII, page 40:
quote.text: […]  And all we met was fair and good,⁠And all was good that Time could bring,  […]

definitions.definition: To be mixed with, to be combined with aspects of.

quote.citation: 1991 September, Stephen Fry, chapter 1, in The Liar, London: Heinemann, →ISBN, →OCLC, section I, page 19:
quote.text: ‘I’m planning a sort of fabliau comparing this place with a fascist state,’ said Sampson, ‘sort of Animal Farm meets Arturo Ui . . .’

definitions.definition: (sports) A sports competition, especially for track and field or swimming.

quote.citation: 2009, Alexandria Mangas, Janet Hommel Mangas, Oxygen for the Swimmer, Xulon Press, →ISBN, page 91:
quote.text: Everyone has to experience their first swim meet. They have to get through their first race, their first DQ (disqualification), and their first miss/scratch of an event. Like all swimmers, my first swim meet was nerve-wracking.

definitions.definition: (hunting) A gathering of riders, horses and hounds for foxhunting; a field meet for hunting.
(rail transport) A meeting of two trains in opposite directions on a single track, when one is put into a siding to let the other cross.
(informal) A meeting.

quote.citation: 2002, George Pelecanos, “Cleaning Up”, in The Wire, season 1, episode 12 (television production):
quote.text: You feel me? You use these phones to set up a meet, go to that meet… and talk face to face, period.

quote.citation: 2004, Matthew Weiner, “Rat Pack”, in The Sopranos, season 5, episode 2 (television production):
quote.text: So what do you wanna do? I wanna be absolutely fucking sure. That's what I wanna do. We arrange a meet. I'll feel him out a little bit.

quote.citation: 2012 February 23, Joe Kloc, “The Case of the Missing Moon Rocks”, in Wired‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: Rosen assured Cregger that he had left no paper trail in bringing the rock into the States. Pretending to be reassured, Cregger agreed to a location for a meet: Tuna’s, a small restaurant and margarita bar off West Dixie highway in North Miami Beach.

definitions.definition: (algebra) The greatest lower bound, an operation between pairs of elements in a lattice, denoted by the symbol ∧.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English mete, imete, from Old English ġemǣte (“suitable, having the same measurements”), from the Proto-Germanic *gamētijaz, *mētiz (“reasonable; estimable”) (cognate with Dutch meten (“measure”), German gemäß (“suitable”) etc.), itself from collective prefix *ga- + Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).

definitions.definition: (archaic) Suitable; right; proper.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i], page 311:
quote.text: It ſeemes not meete, nor wholeſome to my place, / To be producted, (as, if I ſtay, I ſhall,) / Againſt the Moore.  […]

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis 2:18:
quote.text: And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone: I will make him an helpe meet for him.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 8:26:
quote.text: And Moses said, It is not meet so to do; for we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians to the Lord our God: lo, shall we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, and will they not stone us?

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, chapter XXVII, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC, page 131:
quote.text: […]  it is therefore but meet, that in this place we set down who the Pequod's harpooneers were, and to what headsman each of them belonged.

quote.citation: 1958, T[erence] H[anbury] White, chapter VIII, in The Once and Future King, New York, N.Y.: G. P. Putnam's Sons, →ISBN, book I (The Sword in the Stone):
quote.text: The mountain birds are sweeter,But the valley birds are fatter,And so we deemed it meeterTo carry off the latter.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Submissive; passive.
